On Windows, my plan for migrating to a new computer or recovering from a system-corrupting desaster works like this: i have all the folders that store Programs and settings (like c:/program Files; %APPDATA%, %PROGRAMDATA%) on a separate disk.

Upon fresh install, i just copy the folders onto the new system and then i have my programs and their settings back. Only a hardly significant minority of programs actually requires running the installation scripts again.

the goal here is to just "import" all my third party programs and their settings into a new system.

i have done this for several upgrades and reinstalls already and it seems to me like it's the best way to do this.

On Linux, i feel like i can't just do that. 1. User Programs and system programs seem to reside in the same folders

2. different programs seem to use the same folders for their binaries or resources

3. even if i manage to extract all my personal programs and their settings, restoring them to a new installation isn't easy because if i just copy the files, the package manager won't know about them. seems to me like the the package manager is equivalent to window's registry.

Am i wrong? is my whole approach wrong?

the majority of your files and configurations are stored in your /home/[username] directory, so backing up that entire directory (including hidden files starting with ".") should cover most if not all of it. unless you are using root and went out of your way to do something system-wide (like a server - apache, mysql etc.) there isn't a lot outside of /home that you should need to save. I'm not sure what you meant by user program vs system program, as they are all stored in the same location.

for example all of firefox's configuration is stored in /home/[username]/.mozilla, KDE is in .kde, GNOME is in .gconf or something...

once you reinstall your Linux OS of choice copy over the entire home directory.

you would have to reinstall the applications, but that's easy enough with any package manager.

in Linux there's really no "installer" so it's not the same concept as Windows. whatever package manager you use will unpack the package, put it somewhere in /usr, but when you run the application it's going to read from your configuration in /home. there's no such thing as the registry so any user-specific configuration is typically stored in /home/[username]

The hypothetical new installation of Linux will already include some config files in my home directory, setting things to their default values for that distribution. won't copying over my home directory from the old installation likely break those defaults by overwriting those config files?

you would have to reinstall the applications, but that's easy enough with any package manager.

so there is no way around reinstalling every package?

i suppose this could be easy enough with package selection lists.. i know Mint for example allows saving a software list and importing it.

what if my package selection list is from an old version of my hypothetical distribution asks for packages that have been replaced in the newer installation? (because the distro maintainer evolved the distro in a different direction or the package is obsolete)

also, what if the package selection list references packages that i installed locally from .deb files or made myself using checkinstall?

wouldn't necessarily break anything unless there was some major difference in how the configuration is stored, you could just probably overwrite everything.

you'll have to play by ear as to what packages to install. if you're going OS to same OS then you could make a list of packages then pipe that all to yum/dnf/apt-get

the package name I would say is 99% the same in a newer version of a distro (as they have to support upgrades). depending on the distro, some package managers support obsoletes, so if you tried to install an obsolete package name, it would install the newer one.

in a completely different distro, you'll have to play by ear, but they are typically the same or similar. so as long as you had a flat list of packages, you'd probably be okay.

A good practice is having separate partitions for "/" and "/home", usually the first one being just about long enough to hold the system and the installed packages you want and the second one occupying the rest of the space you have available (and maybe also have a third one for swap, but that is a different story).

Then you can copy the entire contents of the user partition "/home" to whatever other machine you want, and having your package-list saved in your user's $HOME directory you will just run the package manager again to install all of those packages.

By the way, package manager is not at all similar to Microsoft's registry - that "registry" is a database of configuration data, the package manager is very much comparable to a version control system.
